title: Why Medicare Advantage Growth Is Increasingly Driven By Special Needs Plans
rawContent:
Roughly 34 million Americans are now enrolled in Medicare Advantage as of 2026, and the plans fueling the most growth are not the standard HMOs or PPOs that most people picture. Special Needs Plans, a specialized category within Medicare Part C, have expanded at a pace far outstripping the rest of the market. For people managing chronic conditions, limited incomes, or both Medicare and Medicaid, this shift matters.

Making sense of SNP medicare plans growth can feel like one more layer of complexity on top of an already complicated system. The plan names are unfamiliar, the eligibility rules are specific, and the benefit differences are not always obvious from a summary brochure.

This article breaks down exactly what Special Needs Plans are, who qualifies, why enrollment is surging, and how to decide whether one makes sense for your situation. The information reflects plan-year 2026 data and has been reviewed against CMS regulatory guidance for accuracy.

Key Takeaways

  • Special Needs Plans are now the primary growth engine within Medicare Advantage, with SNP enrollment expanding at 2–3 times the rate of overall MA growth over the past five years.

  • Dual Eligible Special Needs Plans (D-SNPs) account for roughly 70–75% of all SNP enrollment, serving people who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid, but enrollment is a choice, not a requirement.

  • SNP benefits go beyond standard Medicare Advantage, often including dental, vision, hearing, transportation, and food allowances, though what's available varies significantly by plan and location.

What Are Special Needs Plans and How Do They Fit Into Medicare Advantage?

Special Needs Plans are a distinct category within Medicare Advantage, created specifically for people who have particular health circumstances, not for general Medicare enrollment. They function like standard MA plans in that they cover everything under Parts A and B, and most include Part D prescription drug coverage. But they are built around a more targeted population.

There are three types of SNPs, each serving a different group:

  • Dual Eligible SNPs (D-SNPs) for people who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid

  • Chronic Condition SNPs (C-SNPs) for people with specific serious or disabling conditions such as end-stage renal disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, congestive heart failure, or diabetes

  • Institutional SNPs (I-SNPs) for people who live in or require the level of care provided in a nursing facility or similar institution

Each type exists because a one-size-fits-all plan rarely serves high-need enrollees well. SNPs are authorized to tailor their benefits, provider networks, and care management programs to match the specific needs of their target population.

Beyond the standard Medicare Advantage structure, SNPs layer on additional targeted benefits suited to higher-need enrollees. To understand what those extra Medicare Advantage benefits look like in practice, reviewing your specific plan's Evidence of Coverage is always the most reliable first step.

The Numbers Behind the Growth: Why SNP Enrollment Is Surging

The growth in special needs plans medicare advantage is not a gradual trend, it is a structural shift. According to MedPAC, SNP enrollment has grown at roughly 2–3 times the rate of overall Medicare Advantage enrollment over the past five years. That makes SNPs the primary growth engine inside an already rapidly expanding program.

CMS data for 2026 shows over 1,000 SNP plans offered nationally. KFF analysis estimates 16–18% of all Medicare Advantage enrollees are now in some type of SNP. That share was far smaller just a decade ago.

Part of the explanation is demographic. As the population of Medicare beneficiaries ages and chronic illness rates rise, more people fit the eligibility criteria. But insurer incentives also play a significant role. Health plans pursue SNP contracts because dual-eligible and high-need populations generate higher risk-adjusted revenue through CMS payment formulas. This is not purely altruistic, it is a business model that happens to serve a population with genuine medical needs.

Understanding the broader policy shifts shaping new Medicare changes in 2026 can help you put these enrollment trends in context when evaluating your own coverage options.

D-SNPs Dominate: What Dual Eligible Beneficiaries Need to Know

Among all SNP types, D-SNPs, dual eligible special needs plans, account for approximately 70–75% of total SNP enrollment. The reason is scale: an estimated 12 million Americans qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid, creating a large and growing eligible population with complex health and coverage needs.

A common source of confusion is whether dual eligibility requires you to enroll in a D-SNP. It does not. If you qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid, you can choose a D-SNP, a regular Medicare Advantage plan, or stay with Original Medicare. Each path comes with different tradeoffs around network restrictions, supplemental benefits, and how your Medicaid benefits coordinate.

D-SNPs are designed to bring those two coverage streams together. Many offer coordinated care management, unified appeals processes that cover both Medicare and Medicaid services, and supplemental benefits that standard MA plans often do not include, things like dental care, vision, non-emergency medical transportation, and even food or grocery allowances.

For those weighing whether a D-SNP or another coverage path makes more sense, comparing Medigap versus Medicare Advantage provides a useful framework for understanding the structural differences between your options.

How Federal Policy Has Shaped SNP Design and Consumer Protections

The growth of SNPs has not happened without regulatory oversight. CMS has progressively tightened integration requirements between D-SNPs and state Medicaid programs through 2025–2026 regulatory updates. Plans are now required to implement unified care management systems and coordinated appeals processes, meaning enrollees should not have to fight separately with two different bureaucracies for the same health issue.

These requirements raised the bar for plan entry. Insurers that cannot meet the integration standards are not permitted to offer D-SNPs in certain states. The result is fewer plans in the market overall, but plans that are more operationally capable, which generally benefits enrollees through better-organized care coordination.

That said, scrutiny remains active. MedPAC researchers have raised ongoing questions about whether CMS payment rates accurately reflect actual beneficiary risk and whether enrollees consistently receive the quality of coordinated care that D-SNPs are designed to provide. Enrollment growth and care quality are not the same thing, and regulators are still working to close that gap.

Reviewing Medicare costs in 2026 including premiums, deductibles, and key plan changes, helps you understand the full financial picture when evaluating SNP and standard MA options.

What SNP Benefits Actually Look Like for High-Need Enrollees

All Medicare Advantage plans, including SNPs, must cap your in-network out-of-pocket spending. In 2026, the Medicare Advantage maximum out-of-pocket limit for in-network services is $9,250. SNPs build their supplemental benefits on top of this baseline financial protection, they do not replace it.

In practice, supplemental benefits in SNPs often include:

  • Fitness programs such as the SilverSneakers program, which covers gym memberships and fitness classes

  • Dental coverage including services like dental implants that Original Medicare does not cover

  • Vision benefits including coverage for eyeglasses and routine eye exams

  • Hearing aid coverage a benefit unavailable under Original Medicare; see what hearing aid coverage typically looks like through MA plans

  • Transportation to medical appointments

  • Food and grocery allowances particularly common in D-SNPs

Growth Versus Quality: What the Research Actually Says About SNP Outcomes

SNP enrollment growth is well-documented and continuing. Care quality outcomes are a different story, mixed, still under active scrutiny, and not something to take at face value based on marketing materials alone.

Tricia Neuman of KFF has noted that SNPs are increasingly central to the Medicare Advantage story, particularly as insurers compete for the dual-eligible population. KFF research consistently highlights that higher enrollment does not automatically translate to better care experiences for beneficiaries.

Dr. Melanie Bella, former Director of the CMS Medicare-Medicaid Coordination Office, has emphasized that D-SNPs are designed as a vehicle for integration, but true coordination requires aligned benefits, shared data systems, and genuine collaboration between Medicare and Medicaid programs. Not all plans have achieved that in practice.

When evaluating a SNP in your area, CMS Star Ratings are a useful starting point. A plan's overall rating reflects quality across care management, member experience, and chronic condition outcomes. Beyond the stars, ask specific questions: Does the plan assign a dedicated care manager? How does it coordinate with your Medicaid coverage? What is the grievance and appeals process if something goes wrong?

Frequently Asked Questions About Medicare Advantage Special Needs Plans

What exactly is a Special Needs Plan and who is it for?

A Special Needs Plan is a type of Medicare Advantage plan built for people in specific health situations, not for general Medicare enrollment. The three types are D-SNPs (dual-eligible individuals), C-SNPs (people with certain chronic conditions), and I-SNPs (people in institutional care settings). Qualifying does not mean you are required to enroll, it simply means you have the option.

Do I qualify for a D-SNP if I have both Medicare and Medicaid?

Yes, having both Medicare and Medicaid makes you eligible to enroll in a dual eligible special needs plan during applicable enrollment periods. Eligibility is not an obligation, though. You can compare D-SNPs against standard MA plans and Original Medicare to find what fits best. Review your options for Medicare special enrollment periods to understand when you can enroll or switch.

Why are so many Medicare Advantage plans now SNPs?

Health insurers receive higher risk-adjusted payments from CMS for enrollees with complex needs, making SNP contracts financially attractive. That growth in plan supply can benefit eligible enrollees through more choices and richer benefits. More options also means more comparison work, reviewing Star Ratings alongside benefits is worth the effort before enrolling.

Are Special Needs Plans better than regular Medicare Advantage plans?

SNPs can offer stronger coordinated care and supplemental benefits for people who qualify, but they are not designed for everyone. The right questions to ask before enrolling depend heavily on your doctors, prescriptions, health conditions, and total cost, not just plan type. There is no universal "better" answer here.

What extra benefits do SNPs typically offer beyond standard Medicare?

Common supplemental benefits include dental, vision, hearing aids, fitness programs, non-emergency transportation, and food or grocery allowances. Availability varies by plan and location, so checking your specific plan's Evidence of Coverage is essential. See a detailed breakdown of Medicare Advantage extra benefits to understand what is commonly included.

How does the Medicare Advantage out-of-pocket maximum work for SNP enrollees?

The 2026 in-network MOOP for Medicare Advantage plans, including SNPs, is $9,250. Some SNPs set a lower MOOP as a plan feature, providing additional financial protection for high-need enrollees who use a lot of services. For more detail on how these limits work, see Medicare maximum out-of-pocket rules.

Can I switch out of a SNP if it is not working for me?

Yes. SNP enrollees can switch plans during the Annual Enrollment Period (October 15 – December 7) and the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period (January 1 – March 31). Certain life events or eligibility changes may also trigger a Special Enrollment Period that allows a mid-year switch.

Review the annual enrollment period rules to know your timing options.

Does being in a SNP affect my prescription drug coverage?

Most SNPs include Part D prescription drug coverage as part of the plan, an important advantage for people managing multiple chronic conditions. Always check your specific medications against the plan's formulary before enrolling, since covered drugs and cost tiers vary. Understanding the Part D late enrollment penalty is also worth reviewing so you do not inadvertently create a coverage gap.

Making a Confident Decision About SNPs in 2026

Special Needs Plans, and D-SNPs in particular, are now the primary driver of Medicare Advantage growth in 2026. That fact alone is worth understanding, because it shapes what kinds of plans are available in your area and how insurers are designing their offerings.

Whether a SNP is the right fit for you depends on your specific health situation, your doctors and medications, your budget, and the plans available where you live. There is no single correct answer. The goal is a confident, informed choice, not just picking the plan with the lowest premium or the most recognizable name.

Practical next steps: compare plans on the Medicare Plan Finder tool, review CMS Star Ratings for any plan you are considering, and speak with a licensed Medicare counselor or a SHIP advisor in your state if you want unbiased, one-on-one guidance at no cost.
